The Science behind Zoned

Every workout in Zoned is grounded in decades of sports science research. Here are the physiological principles and key studies that shape our training zones.

Our Approach

All workouts in Zoned are based on established sports science. The intensity zones are not arbitrary: they correspond to real physiological thresholds that can be measured in a lab or estimated from field tests.

Our 6-zone model is derived from key physiological markers: the first ventilatory threshold (VT1), the second ventilatory threshold (VT2, also called the lactate turn point), and maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). These thresholds define distinct metabolic states that require specific training stimuli.

Important: The percentage-based zones presented here are approximations. Heart rate at LT1 and LT2 varies significantly between individuals. Lab testing provides the most accurate boundaries for your personal zones.

The 6 Zones

Z1

Recovery

Marker: Below VT1
Develops: Promotes blood flow and eliminates metabolic waste
Z2

Endurance

Marker: Around VT1
Develops: Mitochondrial adaptations, fat oxidation, aerobic base
Z3

Tempo

Marker: Between VT1 and VT2
Develops: Aerobic capacity and lactate clearance
Z4

Threshold

Marker: Around VT2 / lactate turn point
Develops: Raises anaerobic threshold
Z5

VO2max

Marker: Above VT2
Develops: Maximal aerobic power
Z6

Neuromuscular

Marker: Maximal effort
Develops: Motor unit recruitment, sprint power, anaerobic alactic

Key Researchers & Methods

Stephen Seiler
Polarized training model (80/20)

Véronique Billat
French researcher. VO2max intervals, 30/30 protocol, vVO2max concept

"Intermittent runs at vVO2max" (1999)

View publication

VDOT system and training zones (1933–2025)

Periodization and aerobic base building

Pioneer of the base-building approach

Tim Noakes
Central governor theory

Wildor Hollmann & Alois Mader
Lactate threshold concept origins (Cologne group, 1970s)

Foundational work on lactate metabolism

Oliver Faude
Definitive review of lactate threshold concepts (2009)
